content: The REV1 DNA repair protein is a protein in humans encoded by the REV1 gene. This gene produces a protein that shares structural and functional similarities with the mutagenesis protein Rev1 found in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The Rev1 protein contains a BRCT domain, which is critical for facilitating protein-protein interactions. One proposed function of the human Rev1 protein is to act as a scaffold that recruits DNA polymerases involved in translesion synthesis (TLS), a process that allows DNA replication to continue past damaged DNA. Two alternatively spliced transcript variants of the REV1 gene have been identified, each encoding distinct protein isoforms. REV1 belongs to the Y-family of DNA polymerases and is sometimes referred to as a deoxycytidyl transferase because it exclusively inserts deoxycytidine (dC) opposite DNA lesions. Regardless of the nature of the lesion—whether it is a guanine (G), adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), or an abasic site—REV1 consistently incorporates a cytosine (C). This specificity is attributed to its use of an arginine residue as a template, which complements cytosine effectively. However, it is believed that REV1 rarely utilizes its polymerase activity. Instead, its primary role is thought to be as a protein landing pad, facilitating the recruitment of other TLS proteins, particularly DNA polymerase ζ (Pol ζ), which is composed of the Rev3 and Rev7 subunits. Interactions REV1 has been shown to interact with MAD2L2, a protein involved in DNA damage response pathways. Additionally, it is thought that REV1 may interact with proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) once PCNA has been ubiquitinated in response to DNA lesions. This interaction likely aids in the recruitment of Pol ζ, a B-family DNA polymerase that plays a critical role in TLS.
